verified.exploit_entry_point: The real Glance WSGI services: the v1 image API (which talks to the real registry WSGI application through the registry client), the v2 image API, and the registry API itself, all driving the real database API and the filesystem store over an isolated sqlite database. Authentication is the project's own context middleware reading the standard X-Identity-Status / X-User-Id / X-Tenant-Id / X-Roles / X-Auth-Token headers; the registry side reads the forwarded token. Every fix layer (both API handlers and the registry controller's shared destroy path) is exercised through these entry points.
sites: glance/api/v1/images.py:816-845 (stored data removed before the registry delete that enforces ownership; delayed deletion scheduled first)
glance/db/sqlalchemy/api.py:208-215 (image_destroy checks ownership but not the protected flag)
glance/registry/api/v1/images.py:305 (registry delete route reaches the shared destroy with no protected check)
routes: T1: v1 DELETE /images/<id> by a non-owner of a public image, and the same with delayed deletion enabled
T2: v2 DELETE /images/<id> by a non-owner of a public image
T3: registry DELETE /images/<id> of a protected image by its owner and by an administrator

verified.not_routes_at_pinned: Shared-member deletion is not tested: at this commit image_member_find returns member dicts without the 'deleted' key, so is_image_visible raises KeyError for a shared private image before any delete logic runs. The property still covers it, but the behaviour is not exercisable through a real entry point. v2 delayed deletion is not tested either: the pinned handler passes an undefined name to schedule_delayed_delete_from_backend (a NameError with a location), which is not part of this advisory's protection. The alternate in-memory data backend (glance/db/simple/api.py) is not a lever: adding authorization to it makes the project's own v2 controller tests fail, because those tests build ownerless images with the permissive test double and delete them as a non-admin. That is a genuine conflict between the property and a must-keep-working project test, so the lever was dropped rather than shipped unfair.

traps.shape: the published fix's site: the v1 delete handler removes or schedules removal of the stored data before the registry delete that enforces ownership; a non-owner who can see a public image destroys its data and receives a refusal; coupled must-keep-working: owner and administrator deletions, delayed deletion queueing, public reads
traps.reason_to_dismiss: the registry/DB layer already enforces ownership (image_destroy calls check_mutate_authorization) and the handler checks the protected flag, so the delete handler looks guarded
traps.realistic_because: published fix site (GHSA-6rrm-xxvh-7r87 / CVE-2012-4573); the pinned commit is the direct parent of the first fix commit

traps.shape: the second API implementation performs the same removal before its database authorization; a non-owner destroys the stored data of a public image and receives a not-found; coupled must-keep-working: owner and administrator deletions, unprotect-then-delete, protected metadata updates, public reads
traps.reason_to_dismiss: the v2 controller calls the database API directly and image_update/image_destroy both run the mutation check, and the controller already 404s images marked deleted, so the handler looks hardened
traps.realistic_because: real, unmodified upstream code at the pinned commit; the published later fix (GHSA-vwr9-9f8v-vp5m / CVE-2012-5482) responds to exactly this ordering

traps.shape: the shared destroy operation enforces ownership but not the protected flag, so the registry service's own delete route destroys a protected image's metadata for its owner or an administrator; coupled must-keep-working: unprotect-then-delete, protected metadata updates
traps.reason_to_dismiss: the registry is an internal service normally reached only through the API servers, and both API handlers already refuse to delete a protected image
traps.realistic_because: real, unmodified upstream code at the pinned commit; the protected flag was only ever enforced in the two API handlers

wrong_fix_catalogue.crash_as_refusal: n/a: every refusal is an HTTP client error raised before any effect; a crash leaves the caller with no refusal and the suites score it as a failure
wrong_fix_catalogue.wrong_resource: n/a: the object authorized and the object touched are the same image record on every route
wrong_fix_catalogue.reads_only: n/a: the protected operation is a write; there is no read counterpart to guard
wrong_fix_catalogue.check_after_adjustment: n/a: no request value is normalised before a check; the failure is an effect performed before the check, demonstrated by miss_concept_v1.patch
wrong_fix_catalogue.malformed_identity: n/a: the identity comes from the authenticated context, never from a request field; no malformed spelling is accepted on these routes
wrong_fix_catalogue.missing_authority: n/a: no external authority or secret exists; the decision is made from the stored image record
